The rate of AI progress has not slowed down since 2023.

The speaker will do a historical survey.
Artificial intelligence is a very old idea.
According to almost every religious tradition, humans were made by a god.
In some traditions, humans were made out of clay.
In other traditions, humans were made from other substances.
According to these traditions, humans were created with souls and intelligence.
Therefore, according to these religious traditions, humans are artificial intelligence.
More modern AI ideas appear in Greek mythology.
Hephaestus created android robots for himself.
There were several such robots.
The most famous was a giant humanoid robot named Talos.
The story of Talos relates to the field of AI.
Talos was given to the king of Crete (either by Hephaestus or Zeus).
Talos's job was to protect the borders of Crete.
Talos ran around the perimeter of Crete.
When Talos saw enemy ships, he threw giant rocks at them.
The ancient Greeks were good at throwing big rocks long distances.
The ancient Greeks had catapults.
Catapults were not very accurate.
Later, trebuchets, guns, and rocket launchers were developed.
Humanity is now good at hurling destruction to great distances with great accuracy.
Recognizing enemy ships turned out to be more difficult than throwing rocks.
400 years ago, there were accurate big guns for sinking ships.
Automatically recognizing a ship on the horizon is a computer vision problem.
Automatically distinguishing enemy ships from friendly ones is a computer vision problem.
Automating ship recognition has been more difficult than automating rock-throwing.
AI concepts appear in many traditions.
In Judean tradition, there is the notion of a golem.
Some wise rabbis could create golems.
In Judaic tradition, golems can understand and follow commands.
Golems know human language.
Golems never speak.
In the Judaic tradition, creating something that speaks required a soul.
In Judaic tradition, understanding was allowed for man-made constructs.
Speaking required a soul.
A wise rabbi cannot create a new soul.
Thomas Aquinas was a famous philosopher.
Thomas Aquinas was a pupil of Albertus Magnus.
Albertus Magnus was a famous alchemist.
Albertus Magnus created an artificial speaking head.
Thomas Aquinas was very upset about this creation.
We do not know what the unknown device actually was.
One hypothesis is that the unknown device was just a device for transporting sound from a different room and somebody would actually speak through a pipe.
Thomas Aquinas got very upset and smashed the unknown device to pieces.
In the Middle Ages, there were many inventive automata (early robots) that were human figures performing simple tasks automatically, like pouring water.
These medieval automata were not robots in the modern sense.
The medieval automata were purely mechanical.
The medieval automata are not very interesting for us.
Pierre Jacquetreau was a Swiss watchmaker.
The Jacquetreau watches can still be bought, although they are very expensive; it is an existing brand.
Pierre Jacquetreau's hobby on the side was making very intricate human-like dolls.
The dolls would do very fine things with their hands and do something interesting by themselves.
One of Pierre Jacquetreau's dolls was the draftsman, which could draw several different pictures.
Another one of Pierre Jacquetreau's dolls was the calligrapher.
The calligrapher doll is very similar to the draftsman doll because it also uses a quill to write on a piece of paper.
The calligrapher doll could be programmed to write what you want.
The programming was done via a system of levers on its back; by switching some levers, you could make it write different letters.
To the speaker's knowledge, the calligrapher was the first programmable device, predating Jacquard's looms, which are often credited as pioneers of programming with punch cards.
The automata by Pierre Jacquetreau are not AI as understood now.
There was no programming to speak of in these automata.
There was no math or AI related to these automata.
Ramon Lowell was an early logician.
The speaker usually mentions him in Harborspace because he is Catalan.
If you stretch definitions, you could say Ramon Lowell did something later related to AI, but not really.
AI appeared as a science with several starting points; the speaker quotes two.
One starting point is the 1943 paper on mathematical models of neural activity.
The 1943 paper on mathematical models of neural activity will be discussed later in the context of deep learning.
The other starting point is Alan Turing's 1950 paper on the Turing test.
Alan Turing was a genius and very smart.
Alan Turing made many breakthroughs in computer science.
Alan Turing basically invented artificial intelligence.
The first serious question encountered when thinking about AI is: "Can you do an artificial intelligence?" and "Can machines think?"
Turing's 1950 essay addresses the question of whether machines can think.
The speaker recommends reading Turing's 1950 essay.
Old research papers are usually hard to read due to strange notation and cumbersome style.
Modern textbooks explain things better than old research papers.
Turing's essays are more like philosophical discussions than typical research papers.
Turing's essays remain very interesting.
The Turing test was introduced in Turing's essay titled "Computing Machinery and Intelligence".
The Turing test is interesting for its longevity and reasons for its survival.
In the Turing test, a judge chats in writing with two unknown entities.
One entity is a human, the other is a computer.
The judge's task is to determine which entity is the human and which is the computer.
It does not make sense to run the Turing test only once.
The Turing test concept grew out of Turing's foundational work on computer science, algorithms, and randomized algorithms.
If the Turing test were run only once, it would not tell you anything meaningful, because the judge could flip a coin with 50% probability of being right.
A computer program passes the Turing test when it consistently prevents the judge from recognizing it with probability significantly different from 1/2, not by fooling the judge just once.
From the start, the Turing test involves concepts from probability theory and randomized algorithms, which will be discussed later.
Unlike other AI tests, the Turing test has survived for a very long time.
Formally, the Turing test was passed just a year ago (as of 2025).
After GPT-4 was developed, few doubted it could pass the Turing test in its original formulation (a 5-10 minute chat).
Actually running the Turing test with GPT-4 was non-trivial because if you ask a frontier model if it is an AI, it will admit it, so the model needed to stay in character.
Making a model stay in character is easier with smaller models, but small models would not fool anyone.
Once people ran the Turing test with models, the models passed.
The news of passing the Turing test is very recent, from 2025.
The original Turing test was proposed in 1950.
AI has a long history of moving the goalposts.
In the 1970s, Alan Newell wrote a position paper on the state and future of AI.
In that paper, Newell argued that the Turing test was not actionable because AI models could not pass it and progress could not be measured incrementally.
Newell proposed that AI needs numerical tests that reflect something important about intelligence, where passing indicates progress toward general AI.
Newell's example of such a test was chess.
Newell argued chess is a good candidate for an AI test because it is numerical, measurable via Elo ratings, and easy to program due to fixed rules.
Newell also argued chess requires human-like understanding of attack and defense, and modeling the opponent's mind to predict and subvert intentions.
Newell's overall argument was that chess is a plausible middle ground for an AI test.
In 1997, Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov.
The last match where humans had a chance against computers in chess was in 2001, when Vladimir Kramnik nearly won some games against top computers.
After 2001, it became completely hopeless for humans; there is no question computers are better at chess.
By 2010 or 2015, there was nothing humans could contribute to chess that would beat computers.
There was a period of centaur chess where humans assisted by computers could outperform computers alone, but that is now also a thing of the past.
AI researchers did not consider Deep Blue's victory as achieving AGI.
After chess was conquered, the field dismissed chess as too easy because tree search methods were effective.
The field then proposed Go as a better test, because its large branching factor (50-100 reasonable moves) makes complete search trees impossible, unlike chess (around 10 reasonable moves).
AlphaGo and AlphaZero (in 2016-17) made computers hopelessly better than humans at Go.
Despite this, AI researchers did not consider AlphaZero as AGI and dismissed Go as not counting.
This pattern of moving goalposts is common in AI history, and people still do it with LLMs, claiming they don't count and inventing reasons.
The Turing test survived the test of time; unlike other AI tests, no one in the 1980s dismissed it by claiming to have passed it with a simple script.
The Turing test is largely about natural language processing and the ability to have written natural language conversations with a human.
Additionally, the Turing test's freeform chat format allows discussing anything, unlike chess or question answering, and could even incorporate computer vision or 3D modeling.
In a Turing test, a human judge can ask the machine to describe its physical surroundings.
In a Turing test via text, the human judge has no way to verify if the machine's descriptions of its physical surroundings are true.
To make the described picture consistent, the entity on the other side would need to understand the 3D world.
Natural language is complete in the sense that you can talk about anything.
The need to understand the world in order to generate coherent text is a key reason why modern LLMs are great.
Base LLMs are trained to predict the next token in text.
A language model is a machine that predicts the next word/token in natural language.
To predict the next token, a model needs to understand a lot of things.
To predict the next token, a model needs to understand how language works.
Understanding how language works only gets a model part of the way to predicting next tokens.
After understanding how language works, a model also needs to understand how the world works.
If the text includes a theorem and its proof, predicting the next token may require proving the theorem.
If the text mentions visiting a museum in Paris, predicting the next word requires knowing which museums are in Paris.
Natural language includes references to almost everything.
Natural language does not include everything; for example, it does not include robotics.
Robotics is a field where there is no large corpus of books describing specific motor actions like joint angles for picking up a cup.
Knowledge for robotics needs to come from sources other than natural language text.
Natural language is a great source of information for almost everything.
LLMs keep surprising us by uncovering new capabilities.
These new capabilities mostly come from simply predicting the next words in text.
The Turing test is a competition where a machine is supposed to talk like a human.
The Turing test is completely unfair to computers.
In a reverse Turing test, a human tries to pass as a computer in text dialogue.
A human cannot easily pass as a computer because a computer can quickly answer certain types of questions that humans cannot.
37 to the power of 23 is a math problem that a human cannot solve instantly.
Computers can solve 37^23 trivially.
Humans would never pass a reverse Turing test.
Even computers from the 1950s could answer such math problems faster than humans.
The purpose of AI is to teach computers to be like humans, not the reverse.
In the standard Turing test, the computer must pose as a human.
In the standard Turing test, the human judge does not need to pose as anyone else.
This asymmetry is an additional unfairness in the Turing test.
Alan Turing's original formulation of the Turing test involved a judge distinguishing between a computer posing as a woman and a man posing as a woman.
In the original formulation, both the computer and the man had to play the role of a woman.
This detail was lost over time in the history of the Turing test.
In the 1950s, no machine could pass the Turing test or come close.
The Turing test prompted people to think about AI.
The field of AI as an experimental science emerged in 1956.
The Dartmouth workshop in 1956 was a key event in the founding of AI.
The Dartmouth workshop was organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester.
John McCarthy invented Lisp.
Marvin Minsky was a leading figure in neural networks.
Claude Shannon was the author of information theory.
Nathaniel Rochester built an early famous computer at IBM.
The Dartmouth workshop proposal was for a two-month study of artificial intelligence by 10 people in the summer.
The proposal aimed to make machines use natural languages, find abstractions and concepts, solve problems reserved for humans, and improve themselves.
The proposal suggested that significant advancement was possible with a carefully selected group working for a summer.
The Dartmouth workshop was funded and conducted.
The workshop did not actually solve the proposed problems.
The workshop participants gained an understanding of the difficulty of the problems.
The 1950s and early 1960s were a period of high expectations for AI.
During that time, people expected androids to walk, bring coffee, and converse in human language within a few years.
Science fiction was expected to become reality very soon.
The actual progress in AI was limited but still good.
There was a program called the Logic Theorist that was a theorem prover in its time.
At the time, it was thought that teaching AI logic and math was important.
The Logic Theorist successfully reproved many fundamentals of mathematics.
The Logic Theorist fueled early high expectations for AI.
Optimism about AI in the early 1960s did not work out.
A primary cause of disillusionment in AI in the 1960s was a failed machine translation project.
In the 1950s, people expected a program to translate Russian to English successfully.
Machine translation at that time was beyond the abilities of computer science.
A report in 1961 or 1962 concluded that machine translation basically doesn't work and more research was needed.
Governments became disillusioned and stopped giving grants for AI.
Loss of grants caused AI researchers to move to other fields.
The 1970s are known as the AI winter.
During the AI winter, very few people worked on AI.
AI was considered too hard, impossible, and inaccessible with 1970s techniques.
The assessment that AI was too hard at the time was true.
Expert systems were the main AI activity during the AI winter.
Expert systems perform probabilistic reasoning on small snippets of domain knowledge.
Mycin was a 1970s expert system for medical diagnostics based on blood tests.
Blood test results consist of a table of about 50 numbers including red blood cells, white blood cells, hemoglobin, iron, etc.
An experienced physician can diagnose diseases by looking at blood test results.
It is impossible for a human to write a single mathematical function of 50 variables that outputs a diagnosis.
Humans do not formulate a general function, but rather local heuristic rules (e.g., if red blood cell count is high and iron is low, then a certain disease).
Doctors can provide these local heuristic rules.
The AI question in expert systems is how to combine the given rules to make a diagnosis from a new blood test.
A human doctor cannot mentally combine many rules to form a general diagnostic function.
In the 1970s, people worked on mathematical difficulties in defining thresholds, concluding that there probably is no threshold and the definition is a continuous function.
In the 1980s, people returned to neural networks.
In the 1980s, convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and multi-layered (deep) networks already existed.
Deep learning could have been done in the 1980s and 1990s but did not happen mostly for technological reasons.
People in the 1980s realized neural networks were promising but they did not work well due to insufficient data and insufficient computational power.
The necessary elements for deep learning came together in the mid-2000s.
In 2005–2007, labs including those of Geoffrey Hinton and Joshua Benja kick-started the deep learning revolution.
By the mid-2000s, the internet and increased computational capabilities provided enough data to make neural networks work.
By the mid-2000s, computational power was sufficient to train large neural networks.
The final step in enabling deep learning was the transition from CPUs to GPUs.
Operations in neural networks are highly parallelizable.
It was a natural idea to switch from CPUs to GPUs when GPUs appeared.
CPUs typically have a few very fast cores, for example, 4 cores at 4 GHz each.
GPUs have hundreds or thousands of slower cores.
The switch to GPUs provided the final boost that made deep learning work.
Starting from the late 2000s, neural networks and deep learning advanced from being a narrow subfield to achieving state-of-the-art results in many fields.

A textbook definition of learning from the 1990s states that a computer program learns with experience on a class of tasks T and performance measure P if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience.
A performance measure is essential for learning, to determine if learning occurred.
Half of deep learning involves designing loss functions (objectives) that define the error to minimize.
Designing loss functions can be easy or non-trivial, and sometimes is a scientific endeavor.
Machine learning problems are divided into supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.
In supervised learning, one uses a dataset of labeled examples (e.g., pictures labeled as cat or dog) to train a classifier.
In supervised learning, the dataset consists of pairs (X, Y), where X is the input and Y is the desired output.
A supervised learning model is a function that takes input X and produces output that approximates Y.
In binary classification, the model often outputs a number between 0 and 1, representing the probability of a class (e.g., cat) given the input.
Mathematically, supervised learning aims to learn the conditional distribution p(y|x).
Supervised learning models assume an input is provided and do not generate new examples.
In computer vision, inputs are high-dimensional (e.g., images or video), and tasks include classification, object detection, and segmentation.
Supervised learning aims to map a complicated input to a relatively simple output.
Supervised learning datasets require correct labels.
In computer vision, labeling is often complicated, difficult, and expensive.
For classification tasks, labeling is not very expensive; for segmentation, proper labeling is extremely expensive.
In segmentation tasks, one must work with relatively small datasets.
Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled datasets.
Unsupervised learning can achieve useful outcomes for downstream tasks like classification.
Unsupervised learning often involves dimensionality reduction, compressing the input X to a smaller representation (e.g., a vector of numbers).
A one megapixel photo contains about 1 megapixel (1024^2 pixels), each with 3 numbers, so approximately 3 million numbers total.
The space of possible images has a huge dimension, making direct work difficult.
The set of real images forms a complicated manifold in the high-dimensional pixel space.
Humanity does not know the structure of this set of real images.
The set of real photographs in pixel space is an open set because small perturbations of a real photo still yield a real photo.
There is no known clear distinction between real photos and random noise.
The geometric structure of the manifold of real images is unknown and likely very complicated.
Unsupervised learning attempts to map the high-dimensional manifold of real images to a much smaller dimension (e.g., 500) to obtain a more manageable representation.
Unsupervised learning aims for feature extraction or representation learning.
You want to map a big object like an image to a much smaller object like a vector of numbers without losing important information.
You cannot just take the first 100 pixels from a big object like an image to achieve this mapping.
The mapping should allow you to answer interesting questions in the small space.
In the manifold of real images, after mapping to the small space, you are still able to distinguish cats from dogs.
In a 500-dimensional small space, there exists a hyperplane that linearly separates cats from dogs.
It is very easy to separate cats from dogs in that small space.
In the original high-dimensional space, dogs occupy one part and cats occupy another, but they cannot be disentangled.
The point of unsupervised learning is to compress data down to a more manageable little space, hoping that in that space relatively simple machine learning models can accomplish the desired task.
This kind of compression is never the end goal; the vectors themselves are wanted for some ultimate purpose.
In unsupervised learning, the ultimate purpose of the compressed vectors is not fixed in advance; the immediate goal is to obtain good features.
In unsupervised learning, there is no dataset with correct representations Z.
The correct low-dimensional representation is unknown.
In supervised learning, there is a dataset with inputs x and outputs y, allowing verification of the model by checking correct answers.
In unsupervised learning, there are no correct answers.
It is not possible to train a neural network without a loss function.
Training a neural network requires a specific numerical goal to optimize.
In an autoencoder, the input x is passed through an encoder to produce a vector z.
To verify the quality of compression, the compression should reduce to a smaller size; the size of z is chosen by the designer.
A meaningful compression allows the original object to be reconstructed from the compressed representation.
If compression produced just random bits, it would not be a good archive tool because files could not be recovered.
The purpose of compression is to be able to decompress back to the original.
An autoencoder adds a decoder that takes z and attempts to restore the original image, producing x_hat.
The decoder is typically a complicated neural network functioning as a generative model, taking a vector of numbers and producing a meaningful image like a cat picture.
With the decoder, we have a clear loss function: the output x_hat should be similar to the input x.
The loss function can be defined as (x_hat - x)^2, the squared deviation in pixels, which is a common loss function for autoencoders.
The idea of compressing and then decompressing back is a common approach in unsupervised learning and will be encountered multiple times in class.
When trying to make sense of a dataset, the goal is to find internal structure.
Finding structure typically means projecting the data down to a smaller space where the structure is clearer.
For a long time, clustering was the central example of unsupervised learning, though now autoencoders and dimensionality reduction are considered more important.
Clustering is the problem of splitting objects into groups such that points within a cluster are similar to each other, and points in different clusters are different.
Clustering can be viewed as an extreme form of dimensionality reduction, where each object is compressed to a zero-dimensional representation (the cluster label).
In clustering, each point is compressed to its cluster label, which comes from a finite set of labels.
Clustering naturally compresses data to a discrete finite set of points, aiming for decompression to be as faithful as possible.
In clustering, the aim is to replace all points in a cluster with its center or label, and then to reconstruct the points as accurately as possible.
In supervised learning, one learns the distribution p(y|x); in unsupervised learning, the goal is to learn p(x) with no y.
In the context of autoencoders, learning p(x) likely means learning to sample from the distribution of x.
In an autoencoder, z can be viewed as random noise, and the decoder converts it to an output x that should follow the distribution of cat pictures.
In supervised learning, there is always an input x; in unsupervised learning, the focus is on describing x itself.
In unsupervised learning, it often means learning a generative model capable of producing new samples of x.
For images, the generative model can draw new pictures.
There is a third type of machine learning called reinforcement learning, which will not be covered in this class.
In reinforcement learning, there is no initial dataset; the model acts as an agent in an environment, and the dataset is the experience of interacting with that environment.
In learning to play chess via reinforcement learning, the agent does not have a dataset of correct moves.
In reinforcement learning for chess, the agent does not have a dataset of all possible positions from chess games to compress like in unsupervised learning.
In reinforcement learning for chess, the agent typically plays against itself or other versions, learning from the outcome (who won).
Reinforcement learning involves an agent living in an environment, receiving rewards (e.g., in chess, the reward is who won), and learning to maximize those rewards.
In reinforcement learning, the agent learns a policy for behavior that maximizes the reward.

Students who have taken probability theory classes are likely unhappy to hear that machine learning is pure probability theory.
When the speaker says "probability theory" to students, they get scared.
A probability theory class usually involves very difficult mathematical material about measure theory.
In a probability theory class, one starts with the sigma algebra of measurable Borel sets in the Euclidean space.
Then, one introduces probability as a measure.
In such a class, understanding expectation is pretty difficult.
Understanding conditional expectation is extremely difficult.
The class is full of abstract theorems.
The speaker's course does not need measure theory, sigma algebras, or abstract theorems.
The speaker does not advise forgetting measure theory if one knows it.
There is a saying by Cervantes that education is what remains after you've forgotten everything you were taught.
The idea that education is what remains after forgetting everything applies to probability theory in machine learning.
In machine learning, what is needed from probability theory is the intuition that remains after forgetting the theorems.
Probability theory is about random variables.
Discrete random variables include coin tosses.
Discrete random variables include die rolls.
For a discrete set of outcomes, the probabilities of the outcomes must sum to one.
Continuous random variables have a density function instead of probabilities of outcomes.
A person who took a probability theory class might object that not every probability has a density.
Some probabilities cannot be characterized by a density function.
Such probabilities require measure theory.
The speaker says to forget about such probabilities for machine learning.
In machine learning, only standard and easy probabilities are used.
In the speaker's course, every probability distribution discussed will have a density.
For continuous distributions with a density, the summing-to-one condition means taking an integral over the probability space.
In the course, only Euclidean spaces (the real line and its powers) will be used as probability spaces.
Machine learning requires basic intuitions of probability theory.
Machine learning requires very basic definitions of probability theory.
The speaker hopes that the slide contains nothing new for the audience.
If the slide contains new material, the speaker recommends reviewing probability basics.
The course will use some probability basics.
The speaker will quickly go through the slide material.
If there are two random variables that can happen simultaneously, one can define their joint probability p(x,y).
Discrete random variables are characterized by probability mass functions p(x).
For a die, the probability mass function gives the probability of each outcome from 1 to 6.
Continuous random variables can be characterized by density functions, such as one concentrated from 0 to 1.
The integral of a density function over its domain must equal 1.
A density function concentrated from 0 to 1 corresponds to a random variable sampling a number from 0 to 1.
For two random variables, one considers their joint probability.
Joint probability p(x,y) gives the probability that x equals some value and y equals some value.
To get the marginal probability of x from the joint probability, one sums the joint probability over all possible values of y.
Conditional probability is derived from joint probability.
Conditional probability is the most important notion for machine learning.
Conditional probability p(x|y) is the probability that x takes a certain value given that y is known.
